title: Bedtime sakhis
hookLine: stories of the Gurus at bedtime
tomorrow: Maya's coming to langar with them. what will Fateh hand her?

cards: Nine forty-five on a Friday. Fateh is sleeping over, and he has asked for water twice, the bathroom once, and the hall light left on. Simran's phone is buzzing on the floor.
One video would end this in a minute, and keep him up till eleven. Then he pulls the blanket to his chin and says: Bebe tells me a story about the Gurus. You have to do one too.
Simran knows plenty of sakhis. What she doesn't know is how to tell one so it sounds like a story and not like a lecture.

teach.b: A sakhi is a story of the Gurus, passed down in Sikh families. So Simran picks a small one, the way Bebe told it to her.

teach.h: A WIDE ROBE AND THE FLOWERS.
teach.b: Young Har Rai, who would become the seventh Guru, is walking in a garden in a long, wide robe. The robe catches the flowers along the path and knocks their petals to the ground.
His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, sees it, and doesn't scold. He says, gently, that if you wear a wide robe, you have to walk carefully, so it doesn't harm what's beside you.
And tradition says Har Rai remembered it his whole life and was known for being gentle. That's the sakhi as tradition tells it. Now notice what Simran doesn't do.
She doesn't end with, and the lesson is. She stops. Fateh is quiet for a while.
Then: did the flowers grow back? Then, quieter: was he sad? That's how a sakhi works.
It hands a child a picture to keep, and the questions come on their own, sometimes years later.
Simran could have quoted Baba Farid's salok on ang 1384, which says, in paraphrase, don't break anyone's heart; every heart is a priceless jewel.
She saves it. The flowers already said it.

how: Sikh parents and grandparents tell children sakhis, stories of the Gurus, at bedtime, and the Sikh day closes with Kirtan Sohila, the night hymn.

o: the night hymns sung before going to sleep
a child's prayer said at the edge of the bed
stories of the Gurus told to children at night

games.q: the robe and the flowers — tap the pairs.
p: a wide robe that knocks off petals
walk carefully, so it harms nothing
every heart is a priceless jewel

s: a good bedtime sakhi ends by spelling out the lesson
the sakhi hands the child a picture; the questions, and the lesson, come later.
in the story, Guru Hargobind scolds young Har Rai for the broken flowers
he speaks gently: with a wide robe, you have to walk carefully.
a sakhi is a story of the Gurus passed down in Sikh families
this one is told as tradition tells it.

games.q: a coworker with a five-year-old says bedtime is a battle, and asks how you'd use a story. you say:
o: read a story, then quiz her on the moral so it sticks.
tell one short story, and leave the lesson for her to find.
skip stories; they wake kids up, so just turn out the light.
games.why: Simran told the robe and the flowers and stopped. Fateh asked his own questions: did the flowers grow back? was he sad?

practice: Tell the robe and the flowers out loud, in your own words, as if to a sleepy child: the garden, the petals falling, the grandfather's gentle words. Keep it short, and stop before the lesson.
Then sit with whatever question it leaves you.

wordCard.voice: Bedtime sakhis. Stories of the Gurus told to children at night, with the questions left for them to ask.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sakhi, a story of the Gurus passed down in Sikh families.

carryVoice: Stories at night: tell what happened, and let the child find the lesson. Sleep well.
